review:
There are so many things I love about this game:

1. The combat of this game is so peak, every battle feels engaging with all the abilities at your fingertips.
2. The story for the whole way through so far has had me on the edge of my seat. The lore is fun to get into as well, where I'm spending a lot of time reading the data entries to learn about the world(s)
3. The characters feel really human and endearing, and the writing is really fun. Your party's banter in the overworld and during battles always makes me crack a smile.
4. The landmarks and scenery are always so intricate and beautiful too. The pixel art is just so well done, it makes areas seem so lively and vibrant.
5. The music is killer. I never feel like I get tired of any track because of how well they've been composed for the purpose they serve.

There is so much heart and soul oozing from this game and I've been absolutely digging it.

However... 

My one gripe is the dungeons. I think a lot of other people agree with that sentiment. Some of them overstay their welcome. The challenge in the puzzles is not the problem, it's the slog to get through a lot of them in a row for only 1-2 fights in between. Maybe I'm just impatient lol, but if they were shorter and better paced I think it'd be perfect.

That's one minor nitpick out of the several encompassing highlights, though. Despite that, I do recommend this game wholeheartedly to players looking for a sweet retro style action rpg, or are just looking for a fun new game to try!

I have to recommend CrossCode, because I spent so much time playing it. But I think it's probably not a game for everyone. If this is the game for you then you will love it, but otherwise, you might hate it.

It's basically like an offline MMO. It's actually incredible in its scope, in terms of how much content there is, and how many areas. All the other people in the game are simulated of course. It's a 2.5D isometric world where you attack mobs, interact with NPCs, and upgrade your skills in an enormous skill tree.

It's a purposefully difficult game without mercy. You will grind. There is a difficulty slider which you can use at any time, to reduce enemy damage, attack frequency, or puzzle speed, by 50%. Even if you do that, there will probably be places that you struggle.

But it's a beautiful and interesting world. I found myself really involved in it. It was actually really like MMOs I've played, I got very involved with the in-game world, despite the players not being real. And the story itself — the story you are experiencing first hand — is actually interesting and engaging, and makes you feel involved with it. You will feel sad, you will feel happy. It's surprising how a few sprites and some text can make you feel something, but it can. The artwork is actually really good.

The other aspect of this game are the puzzles. These mostly occur in the dungeons, and while they start out easy, they become very baffling in the mid to late game, and the bosses become increasingly annoying to fight. But for me, it never got to a point where I didn't want to continue. This will depend on your personal frustration level.

Lastly. are the secrets, and I actually loved figuring out how to get them. In this game you can usually see where they are, but because of the 2.5D aspect, you need to figure out how to get to that particular part of the environment, by finding a nearby area that let's you climb up, and then following it around over multiple surrounding areas. I've honestly never encountered that kind of puzzle before, but I found it fun and rewarding to figure out how to get all of the secrets.

Honestly, the game itself was such a joy to play that I would play it with no particular objective in mind.

This game is great, Lea is a very memorable videogame protagonist and the story shows her character and charm alongside others. The combat challenges players in finding enemy weaknesses and puzzles really test the player's intelligence and attentiveness to mechanics and the layout of rooms in order to progress through the story. 

Even if i can keep up with the puzzles and combat, I understand how people can find this game infuriating as the game does not have a difficulty slider, and there are some platforming/ puzzle sections as side content that are genuinely difficult to do and require a lot of patience and skill to complete. 

The second dungeon seems to be a huge filter for players' opinions of the game, as puzzles and rooms can be too many and using introduced puzzle mechanics can feel overstayed as you spend the next hour or so using it when it can be mastered and utilized in half it's time. 

Another mixed bag is exploration, as the game is at a pixelated angled top down perspective, the platforming takes a while to get used to as some cliffs or higher levels isn't as clear to the eyes, making jumping and trying to reach high areas very disorienting and confusing. 

Combining these mixed aspects of the game makes it hard to absorb it in your first playthrough, I had to drop the game because of how exhausting everything felt. Years after, I made a new game and enjoyed it much more because I already understood the game's flow, control and mechanics and was able to skim through puzzles and difficult sections faster. 

Its a story driven singleplayer game that is at heart a puzzle/action game with some action rpg mechanics that unapologetically test the player's wits and time with handcrafted levels, and the MMORPG side of the game is a setting for the story rather than the actual gameplay.

As one review worded, this game is good for the correct players, and i feel that it's bad for anyone that never touched a videogame before because of it's robust controls and complicated puzzles.

[h1]Crosscode[/h1]

This game is impressive in a lot of respects. It very much fits the image of a game you'd find on the SNES only with a content amount near 4~5x that. I'm over 80 hours including the DLC, and if you really wanted to do [b]everything[/b] I could see going even much longer than that. 

The story is surprisingly competent for what it is, with charming dialogue that is a bit goofy, sure, but fits the motif. The world taking place inside of an MMO, you can expect the same kind dialogue you might get, and I will be frank... as someone who has a soft spot for MMOs despite them becoming a bit of a shell of their former self, this game captures the sort of old school 2000~2008 era of MMOs pretty well. Despite it being a single player game, I felt more like I was playing an MMO than most modern MMOs, which is... kind of depressing.

Gameplay wise, I would term this a puzzle game first, and an action game second, even much of the combat intermingles puzzle elements. As far as puzzles go... they're very good. Some are a dexterity challenge, doing puzzles in sequences and sort of reverse engineering what to do, others are a bit more complex, and many outside the dungeons are a head scratcher of platform puzzles of: how do I even get to that chest?

This all works quite well, though I will say the game can be quite punishing for missing a jump or anything else, as you may have to run through multiple zones just to attempt it again. 

Combat is quick, responsive -- a bit hectic and does have a few really annoying designs on some enemies, but overall is quite impressive and complex considering the other elements of this game being so robust as well.

If this game had come out in an earlier era, I would have seen it touted amongst greats like Chrono Trigger, Super Metroid and the like. It's certainly earned the proper title of hidden gem, even if it does have a following, you still never hear of the game compared to others.

If you like puzzles, highly recommend. Just be prepared for the longest 2D action puzzler you've ever played.

总评：
Radical Fish Games 的团队里必然汇聚了一群对像素2D日式RPG抱有极度热忱的创作者，否则完全无法解释如此惊人的游戏体量何以像摩天大厦一般，被一砖一瓦地精心构筑出来。只有遍历游戏内的每一张地图、每一座地牢并最终完整通关的玩家，方能切身领会这种感受。《远星物语》绝对称得上游戏史上最优秀的像素2D日式RPG之一。

主评：
《远星物语》并非传统重主线流程的日式RPG，而更接近旧世代MMO。除去主线的庞大地牢内容外，游戏内还密集分布着大量野外地牢及其对应的关底Boss，这些内容大量充斥于数量庞大的支线任务之中。若非刻意探索或借助攻略，玩家几乎不可能意识到，在某些地图的细小场景或某段看似无趣的材料收集任务之后，会藏着一个体量可观、藏有关底Boss的非主线地牢。笔者感觉制作组在这类内容的引导上存在明显欠缺。游戏内支线任务鱼龙混杂，有时一些看似高大上的长流程任务，实际收益平平且不伴随额外地牢；而有时一些明摆着枯燥的材料收集任务，其后却可能蕴藏着一个规模不小的解谜地牢与关底Boss，当然也可能空无一物。游戏明明握有极其丰富的附加内容，这种弱引导设计却让玩家难以取舍，在耗费时间完成大量无趣的支线前置条件后逐渐失去耐心，进而无法真正聚焦于更有趣的附加内容上。鉴于部分支线任务设计本就平淡乏味，且有滥竽充数之嫌，我并不认为这是制作组对任务回报均衡性的有意尝试，而是游戏引导流程上的一个典型失误。

所以部分玩家其实对这个游戏的定位存在误解。如果将《远星物语》视作一部附加内容充足、但部分内容价值模糊的作品，就像看待《红色沙漠》那样，我想心态理应会放平许多——当然，后者也确未曾于遥远的2018年出现就是了。因此，个人并不建议抱着聚焦主线、长时间连续游玩以迅速通关的心态来对待这款游戏。更推荐每日抽出两小时左右的时间，用于探索收集或完成任务。一旦遇到卡关心生烦躁，大可直接退出，待心态平稳后再回来继续尝试。如此分阶段、长周期、广探索的游玩方式，才是这款游戏最正确的打开方式。若有玩家能以此种方式完整体验并通关，相信你一定能同我一样，深切感受到这部不可多得的佳作那扎实的底蕴与悠长的回味。

【地图方面】
游戏内各分区地图规模庞大，地形垂直交错复杂且细节极丰富，跨地图隐藏收集要素频繁出现。个人非常推荐参照游戏“指南”里【全地图收集流程攻略】中的详细标注地图（其评论栏内有高清版本），在游玩的过程中随时进行隐藏收集与支线任务地点的比对，这样能够极大优化探索体验。由于”引导相对较弱“和”快捷地图显示粗略“等问题，完全不建议盲视野跑路，体验会十分糟糕。

地图上分布的绝大多数怪物在不受到攻击时可与玩家和平共处，仅有少数怪物在贴近时会即时触发战斗，因此基本无需担心平台跳跃式跑图收集过程受到干扰。如遇战斗，脱战后角色HP会在探索中迅速恢复。

另外需要强调的是，游戏内地图探索与跑酷元素深度绑定，虽然其难度对笔者完全构不成障碍（甚至玩的很爽很开心），但这确实是许多跑酷苦手玩家颇为诟病的一个问题。

PS：金色箱子需要在游戏极后期，于涉及波与电两种元素的地牢中获得特殊钥匙后方能开启。如果不愿走太多回头路，可以考虑先通过存档编辑工具直接改出铜、银、金三色钥匙，搜索“远星物语 存档编辑”即可找到相关方法，不会影响正常游戏体验。

【人物性能方面】
游戏内角色近战伤害高但风险大，远程伤害较低，但配合基本无缝的三连闪现，生存风险极小。角色的CP与等级直接挂钩，在资源有限的前期，建议先专精单一方向发展，后期获得刷取经验的机会后再进行双向培养。多元素电路支线开启后，游戏会即时给予足量特殊元素技能点，以供新线路发展。牢记务必学习战技，双并行战技单一线路点满后可无消耗切换。战技可以极大提升刷野怪和boss战的效率，切勿十几级后还靠近远程平A磨死全部怪物。

由于游戏前期缺少恢复资源，建议灵活利用组队角色吸引仇恨趁机输出，敌进我退，敌疲我打。即便能够依靠队友吸引仇恨、灵活走位和堆药瓶将其硬磨耗死，个人也不太建议越级挑战野外Boss，尤其是指剧情前期秋色山野僻静小路中刺畏巢穴的蓝刺畏，虽然笔者仍会不服气地一遍遍去尝试就是了。

【支线任务方面】
随着主线推进，游戏会解锁大量支线任务，其奖励经验对角色的等级提升帮助很大。每张地图的支线任务足以将角色等级迅速提升到应付当前区域怪物的舒适水平。普通材料的收集基本无需刻意刷取，只需在收集地图隐藏宝箱与完成部分支线任务的过程中顺带刷取野外素材和击败野怪即可满足需求。个人不建议非全收集玩家刻意找寻刷取特殊材料，部分特殊材料的位置极为刁钻，加之地图地形上下交错复杂，即便全程对照攻略跑图，也难免有所遗漏。而涉及特殊材料的支线任务，往往需要数种材料，每种数量在十个左右。因此，若已完成一轮较为完整的地图探索后任务仍未达成，大可直接放弃，切勿反复回头刷取，徒耗耐心。另外感到不便的是，每个任务都需要亲自跑回交付才能领取奖励，不过合理的传送点设置在很大程度上弥补了这一劣势。每个阶段的支线任务都会在区域地图中，“探索者中心”的大屏幕上详尽列出，标明发布人物、接取地点、奖励等信息，新任务出现时屏幕右上方也会有提示信息闪过，因此追求全收集时不必担心遗漏。至于找不到任务接取地点或不知如何完成等问题，由于地图信息量庞大且垂直结构错综复杂，我仍建议参照【全地图收集流程攻略】进行细节比对，以有针对性地快速完成。

在支线任务的细节方面，个人感觉虽然数量填充得很足，但半数为跑腿性质的通马桶任务，对主线剧情与世界观的补充也十分有限，其主要价值仍在于获取经验与特殊装备。如果愿意体验，可以挑一些跑图量较低的，或是存在地牢与Boss的支线完成即可；如果不追求支线收集，利用菜单里的降低战斗难度选项仅主线通关亦可。

游戏内还设有逐步进阶的挑战任务，用以考验玩家的操作功底，但其回报率并不高，至少难以引起质变。个人建议简单的挑战可以顺手完成，困难的尝试几次后若感到厌烦大可直接放弃，并非必要内容。

【解密方面】
游戏内的解谜内容围绕角色的弹球能力展开，核心机制仅有直射与镜面反弹这一种解谜手段，并辅以推箱子和元素变换等要素。解谜过程存在时限，时限长短可通过菜单选项进行调整。由于跨场景解谜情形较少，所以只要牢牢把握住这一核心机制，整个流程推进下来会逐渐得心应手。个人其实不太能理解制作组在解谜引导上的弱化处理，即便阶段地牢内解谜手段有限，游戏中的解谜场景往往仍缺乏明确的目标提示，基本全靠玩家肉身摸索、逐步试错，这也是被许多玩家所诟病的问题之一。倘若能够添加更细致的目标指引，我想游戏的整体评价理应会更上一层楼。

具体内容方面，游戏内的冰、火两种元素及其地牢解谜设计较为平庸，难以体现制作组真正的设计水准。本作的精髓主要集中在波与电两种元素及其对应的主线流程地牢上，但这部分内容解锁时间相当靠后，至少需要推进到游戏中后期、累计约25小时左右方能体验，因此对玩家的耐心提出了较高要求。

【剧情】
良。

我始终纠结于一点：主角身为游戏虚拟世界中的一个人工智能AI，若说因程序设计错误而无法说话，尚且可以接受；但在其明显能够理解他人对话内容并进行知识学习的情况下，却仍然无法通过打字、写字或手语等方式进行表达交流，这就很难自圆其说了。尽管后续剧情将其解释为记忆错误与失忆，我仍然觉得这个解释太过牵强，这也是整条剧情线中我唯一无法绕过的硬伤。

除此之外，莉亚很可爱（原来大伙儿都很在意头顶的那两个角呵）。

PS：在此补充强调一句，游戏的DLC内容只能通过好结局进入，官方”新闻“历史内往前多翻翻有详细教程，请参考。

【总结】
综合来看，《远星物语》是一部优点与缺点同样鲜明、且二者同根同源的作品。它的庞大体量、极致的地图设计与海量隐藏内容，既是其无可替代的魅力所在，也恰恰是弱引导、高门槛与内容稀释等问题的根源。这并非一部为所有玩家准备的游戏，而是一部对其受众有着明确筛选的作品。

那些愿意接受分阶段、长周期、广探索的游玩方式，乐于在缺乏明确指引的情况下自行发掘秘密，并且对像素2D日式RPG抱有深厚耐心的玩家，将从中收获一段极其充实且难以复制的体验。而对于追求紧凑叙事、清晰目标指引或迅速通关的玩家而言，这部作品的结构性缺陷则可能成为难以逾越的障碍。

它或许不完美，但那份由创作者极度热忱所浇筑出的扎实底蕴，足以让对得上电波的玩家在完整通关之后，长久地回味。这正是我愿意将《远星物语》称之为“游戏史上最优秀像素2D日式RPG之一”的根本原因——它不取悦所有人，但它所取悦的那部分人，会将它铭记许久。

曾设想，如果这部作品实现3D化，带来的震撼效果应该不亚于《最终幻想7》的重置。但仔细一想，游戏内大量垂直结构的跑酷地形其实很难通过3D形式原汁原味地呈现，便也打消了这个念头。

PS：
（1）我无法理解设计团队为何执意让游戏内的“绿毛龟”角色在主线的必经之路上反复登场。它既非剧情核心，又被强行赋予了一种刻意强化的存在感，仿佛玩家理应对其投入极大关注。宣言对决的机制本身并非不能接受，但将其强行拉长至七回合乃至十回合，便彻底沦为对耐心的纯粹消耗。更让人难以接受的是，每回合结束后对手血量回满而有时玩家状态不满的不对等设计，以及那套疯狂读指令、强行闪避并打出连招的AI逻辑，尤其在其落后两个赛点后，开局直接突脸、疯狗式接战技试图瞬秒的套路，既无博弈美感，也完全丧失了公平感。

一个如此不讨喜、毫无正面回报、只会消耗玩家情绪的要素，竟被三番五次嵌入主线必经之路上，实在令人困惑。这暴露出设计上对“何为游戏的加分项与减分项”存在根本性的认知偏差。对此我只能理解为，这是制作组里某些成员自身人格的深度代入与强烈写照了。

（2）游戏内的“地鼠“，“骨鲨”怪物都是屎。行为逻辑混乱，难以应对，徒耗耐心。

（3）萨......萨菲罗死？

（4）蘑菇王国洞穴潜行任务通关一次之后，如果上方跳台拿宝箱被发现，居然是被传送到最初点而不是最终点？什么意思？还得再跑？这真的不是设计失误？有病。

I don't recommend this game unless you are a big fan of this genre. I have played a lot of video games for over 10 years and some of it is hard for me (although I don't really play rpgs). It is clear the devs made a game for themselves because they love this genre. However, the effects of that are as follows:

-The dungeons take a very long time to complete, multiple hours long, including the first dungeon.
-There is a very long tutorial because there are so many game mechanics.
-The player must execute up to 4 of these game mechanics at once in order to complete the puzzles in the first dungeon, and do it very quickly.

I have finished the Bergen cave dungeon at the time of reviewing this, it seems like the only thing worth doing is the main story, the side quests and side content are mostly boring grind, but there are big rewards for some of them. Trying to find the hidden item in each area is sometimes fun as well.

The Bergen Cave dungeon has puzzles aren't too difficult mentally, but some of them require a really fast execution, so much so that I couldn't figure out a puzzle and had to look up a guide. This is mostly because I didn't realize that I had to do something about twice as fast and thought it was impossible until I read the guide. I recommend slowing down the puzzle speed to 75%, the devs are turbo-gamers and they made this game for an highly skilled audience.

There were also places that I didn't find initially simply because the rooms were too dark, that is just bad design.

The combat is very fun, deep, and has a huge skill tree with many different branches and lots of different abilities to choose from.

I finished the main story without the DLC, so I do not know the full story yet.

Gameplay: 10/10

This is the game’s biggest strength. The combat system is incredibly polished, the progression tree is easy to understand and gradually open up, and the growth in combat power feels genuinely satisfying.

It is simply fun to play this game: running around, fighting, exploring — all of it feels good. Since the game takes place in an MMO setting, it constantly reminds you of that in the right ways. PvE regularly shifts into PvP, and it feels exactly as it should. Dungeons can also optionally be played as a race against your teammate, which is a nice touch.

The builds are varied and actually feel different from one another. You can play just as effectively through damage, both melee and spheres, armor, revenge, and so on.

Level design: 9/10

Excellent. If an area is a hub, it feels like a hub. If it is a desert, it feels like a desert — you can easily get lost and die there. If it is a mountain area, you feel the height, even though the game is top-down. I especially want to mention Vermillion Wasteland, although, unfortunately, the game gives you very limited time there.

As for exploration, most of it comes down to finding the path to optional chests, and almost always this means searching for the exact spot where your character can make a jump. Still, I was rewarded more than once for my habit of sniffing around and fully clearing entire locations. Later on, the game even gives you a chest detector, so aside from ONE STUPID SECRET CODE LOCATION in the Bergen Village, which confused me for several hours, everything is fairly easy to find. The rewards can also be pretty satisfying, especially when they come in the form of special gear.

Story: 5/10

Probably the weakest part of the game. The clichés and general issues of storytelling arised right from the RPG-Maker horror games seem to have migrated here too: at first the story appears naive, but it gradually shifts into something more serious.

I must say, the story is not annoying and can optionally be skipped at any time. At the beginning, the main mystery is still fairly engaging, but the ending leaves a feeling of incompleteness, rush, and a lack of raised stakes. I also felt the game was missing a darker side, even though the potential was definitely there  (Vermillion Wasteland says hi).

In the second half, the story starts to feel like chewing gum, and personally, I was impatiently waiting for the moment when I could finally get back to the actual game. Hope DLC will cover some holes and give a glimpse into darker plot part.

Lore: 10/10

Worldbuilding, on the other hand, was handled much better. The game presents a unique MMORPG world set on a distant planet. In this way, the game is essentially intertwined with reality, although the main story rarely uses this idea. Through notes and encounters, the player can partially dive into the real world behind the game.

The MMO aspect is implemented wonderfully. Other “players” are constantly running around, the main character has a simplified way to communicate with her party, and party members fully participate in battles whenever the game allows it.

The structure of the world feels like a complete game world integrated into a real planetary environment. The world feels alive, even though it is still a “game within a game.” The background lore is fairly deep, and studying it is much more interesting than following the main plot.

The final touch is how the game weaves its own interpretation of the four elements into the island’s locations, which gives the world even more uniqueness.

Art: 8/10

I am also ready to praise the game here. At first, it starts rather slowly and traps you in two fairly similar locations, but later the variety becomes much more noticeable, especially in form of enemy designs. The pixel art ends up being a pleasure to look at and fits the structure of the world perfectly, rather than feeling like a limitation.

I especially want to mention Basin Keep — a full-on noir city in the middle of, yes, a jungle.

The dungeons, except for the first one, fit their elements very well. The skills also look great, especially the wave element abilities.

OST: 7/10

At first, the soundtrack did not impress me much, but by the end, several tracks really stuck in my head and get their way into my playlist. Once again, because of the limited time spent in one particular location, most of the tracks I liked did not get enough room to fully shine.

Thankfully, my favorite Maroon Valley theme played for long enough:)

Overall 9/10

I played quite a bit of this game while going through some fairly challenging health issues, and I often found myself lying in bed playing this game on my Steam Deck, so it holds a bit of a special place in my heart. Although it's not perfect, the gameplay is very fun, the story is fantastic, and I really enjoyed my time with it.

The main story was definitely the highlight of the game for me. The characters in this game are really interesting and well written, and I quickly became invested in their stories, especially the story of Lea. While there's no voice acting, the dialogue is especially well written, and I loved how easy it was to hear the various accents for different characters in my head. The game also made my cry several times while playing through it, which is something that few games have accomplished. Unfortunately, the story outside of the main storyline fell a bit short for me. Most of the side quests follow Lea as she completes quests for various NPCs in the fictional game of CrossCode, and these were usually much less interesting. There's quite a few of them as well, so if you do choose to complete these like I did, there end up being long breaks between portions of the main story. Thankfully, the main story was so good that it kept me motivated to continue playing, even when the side quests were a bit of a drag.

The gameplay is quite fun as well, and the game really starts to open up when you start unlocking different elements and the moves that go along with them. Unloading devastating attacks on massive groups of enemies was extremely satisfying, and they really make you feel incredibly powerful. The puzzles were pretty fun as well, although there were quite a few more than I was expecting, as the dungeons in this game are mostly puzzles. Most of these were pretty entertaining to complete, although there were a few puzzles that felt slightly unfair, as they relied on mechanics that didn’t feel well explained. The platforming was also entertaining, although the perspective definitely made this a bit frustrating sometimes. While I enjoyed times where I had to explore and try and figure out the path to get to a particular area, the number of times I tried to jump somewhere only to realize it was much higher than I thought was quite large, which was unfortunate.

The game looks fantastic, with a lovely pixelated art style, and it generally ran fairly well on both my PC and my Steam Deck, although I did have some issues with stuttering and lag on my Steam Deck. Playing on the Linux-specific version largely fixed this, although this version doesn’t support achievements (they automatically unlock if you switch versions and launch the game though, so it's not a huge deal breaker). Other than that, I didn’t encounter a lot of issues, although the game did crash a couple of times, and I got softlocked at least once as well.

[b]TL;DR[/b] This is a very fun action RPG, with a fantastic main story, great characters, fun gameplay, and amazing art. I did have a few minor issues with the game, such as the much less interesting side quests, a few frustrating puzzles, the perspective making platforming a bit annoying occasionally, and some performance issues on the Steam Deck when running on the default Proton version, but I still had a great time playing through the game, and I'd still highly recommend it.

I think CrossCode was made by and for people with more patience and skill than I have, because for all the thought that was put into all the gameplay mechanics, I just found the game more and more infuriating and not fun the further I progressed.

The dungeons don't merely wear out their welcome. They are the guests that stay too long, eat all your food and leave their rubbish everywhere. The dungeons are INTERMINABLE. So many endless rooms of extremely finicky puzzles, trying to aim quickly and jump accurately and failing while racing against unforgiving timers. I would sometimes spend 1-2 hours in these things only to find I was halfway done. It's exhausting.

The combat has great ideas, brought down by irritating enemy design and pointless limitations. I got so sick of creatures bum-rushing me and interrupting my shots; aiming is already annoying enough without getting constantly knocked back and having to set up the shot again. The elemental overload mechanic is a useless, pointless, irritating constraint that sucks most of the fun out of using elemental skills, and does nothing but waste time during fights where you need to be constantly swapping elements. By Chapter 7 I had turned the damage slider all the way down because combat was making me so angry that I just wanted it over as quickly as possible.

I like the story hooks of CrossCode; I enjoy the way the game-within-a-game setting allows for some really fun metatextual references and jokes. But man, did I ever hate some of these characters. Roughly half of them are the kinds of people I used to avoid like the plague when I played MMOs, the sort of overbearing, overly competitive, abrasive personalities that I tried to minimise interaction with at all costs. Emilie is the worst offender in this regard. I spent the whole game wishing there were an option to unfriend her.

And (minor spoiler in this paragraph) I really hated the stuff with the main character's speech module malfunction. You learn at the outset of the game that your character cannot speak but for a few words, and the reasons for this are explained as the story progresses, but it is never fixed or resolved, and in my opinion the story suffers for the main character's inability to explain what is going on. There are a bunch of misunderstandings and awkward situations that arise because of this, that in the end only served to make me dislike the characters more. and as the game wore on I eventually started skipping all nonessential story dialogue because I was just so tired of looking at Lea's dopey facial expressions accompanied by "Lea! Hi! Wait! Sorry! Bye!"

That said, there are some really nice resolutions between the characters at the end of the story that I enjoyed and appreciated.

Oh and one more thing. Pixel artists, PLEASE. If you're going to create 16-bit style maps that allow us to run and jump all around cliffs and platforms, then you've really got to do SOMEthing that makes it more obvious where platforms are in relation to one another. It is so tedious to have to repeat areas multiple times because there is no way of knowing that the ledge I'm jumping to was higher than the one I was on. This happened CONSTANTLY. I'm a child of the '80s. I love pixel art; it's my childhood. But it needs to be done better than this.

Like I said earlier, I think this game for me is just a matter of unmet expectations and a skill and patience requirement that I do not have. Obviously many people love this game, and it's quite likely that you will too. I'm just glad I saw it through to the end, and now I can uninstall it and not think about it anymore.

Cross Code is an amazing action RPG. I'd say that this is game is the spiritual successor of the ".hack" (dot hack) series, since it has some similar concepts in the worldbuilding alongside a modernized action RPG gameplay.
My favorite aspect of Cross Code is the gameplay. It has a very dynamic and frenetic gameplay that evolves in complexity along the playthrough. Each enemy has its own strategy, which forces the players to adapt accordingly to their opponent. Also, the game teaches the player how to use the mechanics in creative ways not only by bringing up new enemies, but also by giving them puzzles inside the dungeons. It's greatly executed!
Also, when exploring the world, the game motivates the player to always try finding different paths and secrets in order to get better items and equipments and to defeat waves of enemies as fast as possible to increase the dropping rate of items and materials.
The plot itself isn't perfect, but the charisma and dialogues of the party members throughout the game pays off A LOT, they bring the world to life.
Finally, about the soundtrack, it's magical how the music feels nostalgic (?????) even though they are totally original. It gives the vibe of games from the 2000 era, like Ragnarok Online or the .hack series, and I love it with all my might!

love love love love it. The combat feels fun, complex and original. I'm over 100 hrs in and I'm still not consistently using all the attacks. It's definitely an "easy to learn, hard to master" kind of game. If I had to nitpick, I would say dodging can feel a little clunky. I like soulslike games so I'm pretty familiar with I-frames and dodging through attacks, and I'm absolutely awful at dodging in this game. YMMV though, just because I like them doesn't mean I'm a good player.

A lot of people complain about the puzzles, but I think they're incredibly well designed! They're difficult enough that when you walk into a room you think "what is this. how am i supposed to solve this" and then you figure it out and feel like an absolute genius. I honestly didn't think the timing of the puzzles was too "tight" either. The hardest ones only took a few attempts once I figured out the what I needed to do, I don't think I ever "rage quit" a puzzle because it was frustratingly close timing.

The story is good, the characters are cute, and the dialog is light and funny, and satisfyingly meta (its a game about a game, you gotta). Do I think it's a literary masterpiece that deeply explores the nature of the human mind? No. Well, okay, a little. Did I cry like a little weanie multiple times? Yes. AM I a little weanie? Also yes.
